entry.title: Jensen Huang’s Biopic Feels Inevitable — The Right One Might Be Impossible
entry.summary: Jensen Huang's affairs and Nvidia exit scream Hollywood, but 'Artificial' and 'The Social Reckoning' tell us why tech dramas struggle to keep up.
entry.content:
Hollywood loves a visionary, especially one whose biggest gamble eventually made him a billionaire. But the trouble with making a biopic about a tech mogul actively shaping the future? That kind of story often refuses to sit still long enough to be told before ending in calamity.

When it comes to Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang, any filmmaker hoping to get ahead of the microchip company’s uncertain next chapter may already be too late. Or is it still… too early?

On Thursday, Nvidia announced that Huang had resigned as CEO and board member, effective immediately. And no reason was given for the departure: a rather extraordinary development for someone who helped build the company into one of the most powerful and lucrative forces in artificial intelligence. For Hollywood, it’s the kind of twist that practically demands a screenplay.

Related Stories
Miles Teller Opens Up About ‘Paper Tiger,’ Adam Driver, and Losing His Home Before Filming James Gray’s Movie
Fall Festival Movies Sold: ‘Woman Unknown,’ May el-Toukhy’s Golden Lion Winner, Sells to Cohen Media Group

Huang’s rise from teenage Denny’s employee to the face of the AI boom always had the makings of a prestige drama. Now there’s a corporate disaster — involving an alleged Chinese espionage operation and reports of multiple extramarital affairs — at the end of it. Hot dog! Still, it’s anyone’s guess whether that fiery conclusion can seem genuinely relevant by the time film and TV creatives get around to adapting it.

The entertainment industry has spent much of 2026 demonstrating how difficult it is to dramatize Silicon Valley while the real people involved keep making headlines. Aaron Sorkin’s “The Social Reckoning,” for example, opened to just $5.5 million in North America. That’s a disappointing debut for the follow-up to David Fincher’s “The Social Network,” which won three Oscars including best adapted screenplay.

Revisiting Facebook through the perspectives of whistleblower Frances Haugen (Mikey Madison) and Wall Street Journal reporter Jeff Horwitz (Jeremy Allen White), Sorkin attempted to turn Mark Zuckerberg (Jeremy Strong) and his social media platform’s disastrous effects on politics and public discourse into a satisfying sequel.

Of course, audiences had already spent years living with the very real consequences of Zuckerberg’s company’s actions. And in his “D+” review for IndieWire, Ryan Lattanzio described Sorkin’s approach as “less old-fashioned than completely out of date,” criticizing a falsely triumphant finale that failed to reconcile how little had actually changed in the world after the investigation’s revelations came to light.

While Sorkin was late to the party, Luca Guadagnino’s “Artificial” has had the good fortune of arriving right as things have been starting to get worse. Dramatizing OpenAI’s chaotic 2023 firing and rehiring of Sam Altman (Andrew Garfield), the dark comedy finds absurdity in the gap between Big Tech’s grandiose promises and the frequently clownish folks making them.

In his “B-” review for IndieWire, David Ehrlich praised the coming film for recognizing how “deeply fucking stupid the road to superintelligence has turned out to be.” He also questioned its tendency to simplify an ongoing story into something more resolved than it is. (Suffice to say, any film that tries to predict the cultural conversation also risks declaring history finished too soon.)

“Artificial” has benefited from some remarkable timing, too. Amazon MGM dropped the project after entering into a partnership with OpenAI — with sources telling the Los Angeles Times that the script’s critical perspective on artificial intelligence specifically contributed to the decision. Neon eventually acquired it, and a well-received New York Film Festival premiere helped build some serious awards-season momentum for routine Oscar contender Guadagnino.

Then came the U.S. midterms, during which voters across the country backed restrictions on data-center development. That makes the questions about who controls AI and who actually pays for its consequences feel spectacularly urgent, effectively turning a simple boardroom fight into a existential consideration of society with significantly heavier stakes.

Of course, tech biopics don’t necessarily have to predict the future to be powerful.

Consider Hulu’s “The Dropout,” which won Amanda Seyfried an Emmy for playing Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes. Four years later, Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s boundary-breaking documentary “You Can See Everything” once again made Holmes a viral sensation — even bringing Seyfried into contact with the woman she portrayed.

As IndieWire TV critic Ben Travers recently argued, “The Dropout” remains effective precisely because it didn’t pretend to know everything about Holmes in 2022. Fielder and Oppenheim’s contribution often gets so close to its subject that Holmes’ motives become difficult to pin down, while the series maintains enough separation to keep her actions and victims in focus.

“Sometimes a healthy distance provides greater clarity,” Travers wrote.

That’s a useful lesson for anyone hoping to next adapt the life of a Silicon Valley billionaire before history has finished passing judgment on them. And in Huang’s case, there’s already plenty of material to work with — before pretending to know how his former employer’s whole saga ends.

Having cofounded Nvidia in 1993, Huang nearly lost the company after betting on a method of rendering video-game graphics that Microsoft effectively rendered obsolete. With Nvidia running out of money, he then scrapped its original technology and made a last-ditch gamble on a new chip that ultimately helped save the business.

Huang eventually helped develop the graphics-processing infrastructure that would make his company’s hardware essential to the AI boom. Fast-forward to a public apology to his wife and throw in a leather jacket? Hollywood could probably have a trailer ready by Christmas.

But that would also be the easiest, and potentially least interesting, version of Huang’s story, right? Nvidia’s success was built on the backs of countless engineers, researchers, and developers aside from Huang. The fallout within the AI giant will impact everyone.

A truly great movie about Huang and Nvidia would need to understand the company’s founding and survival, follow the enormous risks Huang took with that future, and then seriously interrogate what happens when a single corporation becomes indispensable to the technology rapidly reshaping nearly all of modern life. Those are three(!) very different artistic ambitions. Considering the entertainment industry’s own increasingly lucrative partnerships with AI companies, and Amazon’s offloading of “Artificial,” there’s reason to wonder just how much scrutiny Hollywood would be willing to apply to the innovators they are in business with.

Which brings us back to the question of when to make a Jensen Huang biopic.

The tech industry is moving faster than filmmakers can reasonably hope to keep up with, but the bigger problem may be that news around the Silicon Valley story most worth telling is changing just as quickly. A film about the man who helped build the future we’re facing might have been an easy sell a few years ago. These days, the more pressing issue is what kind of world Huang actually put in motion — and whether Hollywood can afford to doubt it in public.

entry.title: Miles Teller Opens Up About ‘Paper Tiger,’ Adam Driver, and Losing His Home Before Filming James Gray’s Movie
entry.summary: Miles Teller talks his role in James Gray's 'Paper Tiger' and more. Interview.
entry.content:
[Editor’s note: This interview was originally published during the 2026 Cannes Film Festival. Neon will release “Paper Tiger” in theaters on Friday, November 6.]

An actor who started at 22, Miles Teller earned rave reviews out of the gate for his debut performance in “Rabbit Hole,” when he was signed swiftly by CAA, followed by “Whiplash” and “The Spectacular Now.” He has worked steadily ever since, with everything from auteur fare like “Whiplash” and studio franchises such as “Divergent” and “The Fantastic Four” to his name. Holding his own opposite Tom Cruise in the blockbuster “Top Gun: Maverick” pushed him into the limelight, but he was still playing Rooster, the son of radar intercept officer Nick “Goose” Bradshaw (Anthony Edwards).

Related Stories
Fall Festival Movies Sold: ‘Woman Unknown,’ May el-Toukhy’s Golden Lion Winner, Sells to Cohen Media Group
Saoirse Ronan Has Wanted to Direct Since She Was a Kid, and Her Exquisite First Short ‘Paper Plane’ Proves She’s Got the Goods

His latest role in James Gray’s “Paper Tiger,” which earned raves at Cannes, sees Teller play a real grown-up, Irwin Pearl, a Queens engineer and family man opposite Scarlett Johansson as his wife Hester, and Adam Driver as Gary, his older brother, a former cop. No longer the onscreen son of a leading man, Teller is now firmly in father roles. Irwin is slowly building a solid business when his brother offers a quicker route to success. Alas, the naive Irwin goes for the idea and, during an unscheduled night reconnaissance, blunders with the Russian mafia, seeing things he should not see.

I sat down with Teller at the Carlton Hotel in Cannes after the movie wowed in its world premiere. He was seeing it for the first time. We do not count fake standing ovations at IndieWire, but I was there and can vouch that it played well. The dynamic between Driver and Teller is powerful, with Johansson holding her own in the middle. Even though the movie did not land a Cannes prize, it will play the fall festivals and enter awards contention.

The following interview has been edited and condensed for clarity and length.

Anne Thompson: You’ve played the Cannes game before.

Miles Teller: I’m one of those actors [where] it’s pretty hard to watch yourself. I always have a hard time. I was here with Nic [Winding] Refn for this limited series that we did [“Too Old to Die Young”]; that was my first time at Cannes. I’ve done Cannes with “Maverick.” It’s truly an overload of the senses.

You’ve never given this kind of performance before.

Hopefully, your taste evolves as you get older. It struck me that on my first film, “Rabbit Hole,” I was playing the wide-eyed teenager, and we filmed the majority of that movie in a house in Queens. And now I’m playing the part of the parent.

That was your breakout. You revealed some strong emotions related to your own car accident. I’m so sorry you lost your home in the Palisades Fire.

When I met James for this movie, our house had just burned down. And I had just lost my grandfather. We were renting a place in Santa Barbara, and then I got the call saying James wanted to meet me for this. That infused this story and performance with a lot of love as well, because of that feeling of home that Keleigh [Sperry] and I had lost. I’d lost it with my grandfather, but then also just the physical place where you can have people come gather, where you have memories attached. We did not have that, so that probably came through.

Do you believe that you have to grow up a bit before you can find your way in Hollywood?

If you want to have a long career, the audience, hopefully, that you attract in your early 20s, as they get older, and they start having kids or not having kids, but just getting more life experience under the belt, you want to reflect that in your choices as well. And James makes movies for adults, he deals with characters. I’ve loved every one of his films, and I’ve always felt like he gets incredible performances, so I was excited to play a man at this point.

Every actor is going to get to a place where you know it’s tough because you do something that has some success to it, and then people want you to keep doing that same thing, whether that’s from the studio side or you keep getting scripts that are that same kind of thing.

What was your pigeonhole?

When I started out with “Rabbit Hole,” and then I wanted to audition for comedy, they’re like, “he’s not funny.” And then you do comedies, and you want to be going back to drama, and they’re like, “Willard from ‘Footloose,’ what are you talking about?”

I remember “Bleed for This.” [He gets up to close the shutters to block the noise for my audio, and pours me some water.] That was a point where I was 27, and I said, “OK, I want to step up and play, not the funny friend. Playing Vinny Patz, as a five-time world champion boxer, very much a man’s man, absolutely, that was something. But it always comes down to a director, oftentimes taking what I feel is a chance on me, casting me in a role that I haven’t necessarily shown those abilities before, but believing that I could do that.

You had to carry the TV series “The Offer,” in which you play Al Ruddy, who produced “The Godfather,” running interference between Francis Ford Coppola, Robert Evans at Paramount, and the mafia. That must have been tough.

I was intimidated by portraying Al, to be honest with you, not just his bravado and accomplishments, but it felt like I was playing somebody who had more life experience than I had at that point, and there was a certain maturity to that. I enjoyed that Al, being a man of action, if he takes a step back, he’s taking two steps forward. Typically, there’s five or six different producers doing all these things: that was all Al.

In “Paper Tiger,” there’s one scene between you and Adam Driver where you get into a fight. Your face was shaking with anger.

I know. I saw that. Yeah, there was a twitch going on there. At least in my own life, your family can get to you in a way that nobody else can. Those feelings are so deeply rooted and established from childhood, so I guess in that moment, and neither one is fully aware of the ramifications of the Russians, this deal going bad, and how it’s affecting that person in their life. In that particular scene you’re letting out. It’s not just about what they’re talking about right there. It’s an entire lifetime of misgivings — he’s going to let him have it. When that’s happened to me in my personal life, you feel so bad afterwards. It’s a horrible feeling when you’re not talking to a sibling or your parents, and often it’s hard to make amends.

How did James Gray base this film on his own father’s experience?

With his father, that was the biggest regret. He took it to his deathbed, the fact that he brought this [danger] into his home, and his family became collateral damage for his business ambition. [In the movie] the venture that he went into, to go into business with his brother, he makes a mistake that was very naive. I think it’s easy to forgive this mistake. When I read this script, I had a ton of empathy for this family in this situation, and then also what Hester is going through.

Did you have any models for your character in this movie? Your own father was an engineer.

No, he was a project controls manager, but worked nuclear. The men that I grew up around, my father and my grandfather, were strong men, but very sensitive, and were dependable, reliable. My grandfather was married to my grandmother for 60-something years. I never saw her open a door for herself. I never saw her carry her own bag. He was a Marine, but he also was well-versed in world history, and he was a sweet man who was never afraid to show that side of him, but he also would stand up for himself, or his wife, or his kids, whatever it is. He took a lot of pride in that.

I found it refreshing, even comforting, to watch a movie about a kind, loving family man who’s good at his job, who’s competent. He’s a good dad. You haven’t shown that side to such a degree.

I felt immensely for this father and husband. It was clear he loves his kids, and he’s trying to lead by example, and to show them that success in life is not based on the car you drive. He wants to show them that you can build something on your own merit, and if you work hard and treat people right, that you can earn it.

Those values are no longer as respected as they once were. So, if you were to look back at your career, you did some studio work, like the “Divergent” series. Have you made a course correction? That comes with maturity, too, when an actor recognizes what they want to do rather than doing what people tell them to.

Early on, I didn’t want to feel like I was repeating what I had just done. I didn’t want people to be able to expect what I was going to do next. I always want to defend young actors in their careers, because people say, “Oh, why did you make that choice? Why did they make that choice?” You’re just hoping to get a role, and it’s less than 10 percent of people in SAG who pay their bills off acting alone. We all want to work on the best material with the best directors and the best actors. There’s an ebb and flow. I used to be more critical of work other people were doing, because you get thrown into this rat race when you’re first starting out.

Who were you competing with? Who was in your class?

It was me, and Michael B. [Jordan] and [Robert] Pattinson and Shia [LaBeouf] and [Zac] Efron was big, “The Hunger Games” stuff was blowing up. As I’ve gotten older, I appreciate and have respect for longevity, if you can hang around. I always wanted to contribute. When I was going to the Lee Strasberg Institute at NYU, and looked on the wall, there’s all these incredible actors that went through there. I hold acting and actors in such high regard, whether it’s theater or film or TV.

You seem to be delivering performances at such a level that you keep getting more work. The work itself is selling you. You had to counteract some bad press. Did that hurt you in terms of getting roles?

That was so mishandled. The reason why I have not done profiles is because I said, “Wow, if I’m not doing this interview on camera, this person can misquote things or put things out of order or say things that didn’t happen.” It felt like such a violation of what actually transpired. I told my team, “Guys, I don’t think I’m doing this again, because I’m reading this and this doesn’t sound like me to me. This is not life, so why would I ever want to be a part of something where they can just put that in?” So it’s unfortunate that being a good person, that doesn’t sell. People want to click on the negativity. If you go to bed and put your head on your pillow and how you treat people truly, that’s what matters. That [2015] interview was like 12 years ago.

Some people still remember. Well, casting directors know who you are and what you can do.

The actors, the directors, the crew, the producers, you can’t hide who you are when you’re on set.

Legal questions surround the Michael Jackson estate and his lawyer, John Branca, who you play in “Michael,” which has grossed $707 million worldwide. What’s going on with the sequel?

They had to rework the third act of the last movie. As far as the sequel goes, I know they’re working on it. I haven’t had any direct discussions, other than the team is excited to complete that story.

entry.title: ‘The Good Daughter’ Review: Rose Byrne Sizzles in Peacock’s Brutal Trauma-Drama About Crime-Solving Sisters
entry.summary: In 'The Good Daughter,' the clichés stack up nearly as fast as the cast can distinguish them, but Rose Byrne and Brendan Gleeson hold it together.
entry.content:
Peacock‘s latest limited series “The Good Daughter” adds to the streamer’s solid run of women-led thrillers, though it’s best to interpret that label loosely. When stretched to include biographical mysteries, the streak dates back to 2022 with Nancy Oliver’s limited series “Angelyne,” showrun by Allison Miller and starring Emmy Rossum as the enigmatic ’80s era L.A. personality known only by her mononym (until some man decided that’s not good enough).

Then came a slight pivot into pulpy book adaptations with “Apples Never Fall” (2024) an adaptation of Lianne “Big Little Lies” Moriarty’s novel of the same name that was showrun by Melanie Marnich and centered around a wealthy family’s missing mom, played by Annette Bening. Not only did “Apples Never Fall” make the perfect amuse-bouche for Peacock’s next whodunit — “All Her Fault” (2025) the Emmy-nominated yet deeply unserious Sarah Snook showcase — it also teed up Jake Lacy, Hollywood’s leading expert in the field of “entitled douchebags,” for a meta-fun Keyser Söze moment as the devil hiding in plain sight (while his wife took on all of their family’s emotional and physical labor).

Related Stories
‘American Doctor’ and ‘You Can See Everything’ Lead 2027 Cinema Eye Honors Film Nominations
‘Ebenezer’ Review: Johnny Depp Is Absolutely Insufferable in a Dull and Dreary Christmas Carol

Two less successful entries, by viewership anyway, were this year’s jaunty critical favorite “Ponies,” from co-creator and director Susanna Fogel, which starred Emilia Clarke and Haley Lu Richardson as the CIA’s first female spies operating within the Soviet Union; and the jaundiced “Long Bright River” (2025), a limited series co-created by Liz Moore (who wrote the novel on which it was based) and Nikki Toscano (who served as showrunner), starring Amanda Seyfried as the only cop in a bad/pale part of Philly who cares about neighborhood sex workers and opioid addicts getting killed (one of whom may turn out to be her missing sister).

All of these shows share common tropes, despite disparate tones, topics, and objectives — not the least of which are their glorious feminist underpinnings. Within each of these thrillers lurk so many shady husbands, brothers, bosses, and dads. The patriarchy looms large enough to get name-checked, and the leading ladies are all fighting an uphill battle just to be seen, heard, and understood. “All Her Fault” was so attuned to the ways men routinely let down their families Vulture hailed it as a “misandrist masterpiece.”

But “Long Bright River” carries the most direct parallels with “The Good Daughter,” both by design and on accident. They’re both gritty and dark. They both follow leads whose careers connect back to their personal demons, and they both track working-class women fighting for their impoverished communities (and against the shitty men who run them). Where “All Her Fault” and “Apples Never Fall” could be carelessly devoured as melodramatic amusements, “Long Bright River” and “The Good Daughter” are too brutal and self-serious to constitute anyone’s idea of a “fun” binge, even if there is a morbid bit of fun to be found in the latter’s performances, dialogue, and many, many character quirks.

“The Good Daughter” is set in the fictional town of Pikesville, GA, where Charlie (Meghann Fahy) works as a public defender, adjacent to her sole-surviving parent, town pariah, and private defense attorney, Rusty Quinn (Brendan Gleeson). Her mother, lovingly referred to as Gamma (Olivia Williams), didn’t live long enough to be a grandma; she was murdered in front of her daughters when they were just kids, and the resulting assaults left Charlie’s sister Sam (Rose Byrne) with a lifelong motor speech disorder called dysarthria, as well as impaired vision and a notable limp.

Sam is also a lawyer, but she specializes in patent law (to avoid the anxiety that comes with criminal cases) and moved to New York as soon as she was old enough to get out of Georgia. She only returns to Pikeville when Rusty, for the first time, calls to say her sister needs help. Why now? Well, the list of Charlie’s hardships is nearly as long as her sister’s, but Rusty — who tends to speak in Flannery O’Connor quotes — is likely referring to the most recent trauma: a school shooting she witnessed that left the principal and a 13-year-old student dead.

Charlie’s poorly timed visit to the local grade school and a flashback to her mother’s horrific murder take up the first 15 minutes of the premiere, which may be enough to scare off subscribers who tuned in expecting something closer to Peacock’s other thrillers. For those that stick around, “The Good Daughter” steadies itself for the bulk of its six-episode run.

Once Sam is back in town, the two sisters start mounting a defense for their dad’s client: the school shooter, Kelly Wilson (Shayna Benardo), an 18-year-old student with an intellectual disability. The maniacal powers that be are eager to kill her — first at the scene of a shooting, where a teacher (played by Jake McDorman) saves her from the trigger-happy cops, and then in court, where a self-righteous district attorney argues for the death penalty, competency laws be damned.

They’re all under the Coins’ thumb, a powerful family (with connections throughout the local government) who turned the township against Rusty and his family long ago. Everyone believes Charlie and Sam lied about who killed their mother, and they resent Rusty for defending so many “obviously” guilty parties. The only folks willing to help the Quinns are Rusty’s best friend and legal aide, Lenore (Harper Steele), and Charlie’s husband and assistant district attorney, Ben (Michael Dorman). Otherwise, they’re on their own, standing up for Kelly, standing up to the Coins, and standing against Bad Men™️.

Adapted by Karin Slaughter (from her own book) and directed entirely by Steph Green (“Duster,” “Dare Me”), “The Good Daughter” holds back too many revelations for the finale, creating an exposition-heavy ending that covers its bases but functions like an endless list of answers. It’s not as powerful as it needs to be in order to justify its upsetting subject matter, and it’s trauma-drama plotting skews into overkill well before it’s done doling out distress.

And yet, I have to say, much of it works. Credit goes to the cast, particularly Byrne and Gleeson, for internalizing their showy character quirks to such a degree that Sam’s limp, vision impairment, and sporadic stutter — yes, also a stutter! — never feel like her defining traits. The same goes for Rusty’s folksy banter, poetry quotes, and even his red-nose routine, in which the professional attorney pops on a clown nose whenever he feels the moment calls for a little levity. Such a strange, impractical choice, deployed as often as it is here, could spoil a curious character who’s always viewed from his children’s removed perspective. Maybe he’s unbelievable, maybe he’s too cute for the rest of the story, maybe he’s simply too silly. But Gleeson gathers it all up to form a heartbroken widower who just wants to give his traumatized children the light they need in an ever-darkening world.

Fresh bursts of creative Southern witticisms are similarly rewarding, like hearing Gleeson say, “Never kick a fresh turd on a hot day” or Byrne tell a patronizing windbag “to shit in both hands and start clapping.” The series ultimately rests on Sam and Charlie’s relationship, and their relationship is strong. Their dialogue, particularly when poking fun at one another, rings true, and there’s a buddy-cop dynamic to their investigation that demands to be extended into an ongoing series.

Not this series, mind you. Peacock should limit this limited series to its established, er, limits. But I know a streamer where Byrne and Fahy could pitch another thriller centered around two crusading women looking to crack a case, save their souls, and destroy the patriarchy in one fell swoop.

Just maybe base the next one on a slightly easier read.

Grade: C+

“The Good Daughter” premieres Thursday, November 12 on Peacock. All six episodes will be released at once.

entry.title: Fall Festival Movies Sold: ‘Woman Unknown,’ May el-Toukhy’s Golden Lion Winner, Sells to Cohen Media Group
entry.summary: Movies like 'Babies,' 'Ink,' and 'Elsinore' have already sold to distributors ahead of their world premieres at TIFF, Venice, and Telluride.
entry.content:
What will the buyers be snapping up at the fall festivals? With this year’s Toronto International Film Festival already touting a high number of premieres for movies that originally bowed at Cannes or Sundance, there’s fewer world premiere sales titles that aren’t already with distributors than we’re used to. Still, the festival (with its very first market in place), plus Telluride, Venice, and New York are loaded with options, and there’s always the potential for another historic breakout like last year’s “Obsession.”

We’ll be tracking all the sales as they come in here, so check back frequently.

Films Acquired After the Festivals

“Woman Unknown”

Distributor: Cohen Media Group
Director: May el-Toukhy
Festival: Venice Competition
Buzz: Venice’s top prize winner of the Golden Lion has found a U.S. deal, this one made out of AFM with Cohen Media Group. Not only did el-Toukhy (“Queen of Hearts,” “The Crown”) movie win the Golden Lion this year, star Mathilde Arcel also won the Volpi Cup for Best Actress. The Danish film, also Denmark’s official Oscar selection, is a period drama set after World War II about a former housekeeper now set to be married to the household’s wealthy patriarch. But as she plans an extravagant dinner party to celebrate the occasion, hidden aspects of her past begin to resurface. Namely, it has to do with Danish witch hunts of those associated with Nazis after the war, and our positive review called it an “angry, despairing film” with a “Haneke-level bleakness in its assessment of human nature.” Cohen Media Group also recently bought an Isabelle Huppert comedy called “All About Corinne” that played at TIFF and premiered at Locarno.

Related Stories
‘American Doctor’ and ‘You Can See Everything’ Lead 2027 Cinema Eye Honors Film Nominations
What Makes a Good Oscar Campaign? Just Ask Sony Classics’ Michael Barker and Tom Bernard

“The Julia Set”

Distributor: Sony Pictures Classics
Director: Niki Byrne
Festival: TIFF Special Presentations
Buzz: Sony Pictures Classics have acquired all rights in the United States, Benelux, Switzerland, Italy, Scandinavia, Spain, United Kingdom, Eastern Europe (excluding Poland), Australia, New Zealand, South Africa, Israel and Asia (excluding Singapore) to “The Julia Set,” written and directed by Niki Byrne. The film had its world premiere at this year’s Toronto International Film Festival and follows a gifted young math prodigy (“One Battle After Another” breakout Chase Infiniti) who is “recruited into an elite prep course culminating in the most punishing exam in mathematics, while at the same time falling into a romantic relationship with her charismatic teaching assistant, Pascal (Christopher Briney).”

“The Daughters of Abraham”

Distributor: Strand Releasing
Director: Hanaël El Yousfi
Festival: TIFF Discovery
Buzz: This directorial debut follows two friends, one Muslim and one Jewish, spending a carefree summer in Marseille, only to see the expectations and tensions between their traditional families start to get in the way of their friendship and leads them to take hold of their own destinies. El Yousfi both wrote and directed the feature, co-writing it with Raphaël Chevènement and Mia Grace Brown. It had its international premiere at TIFF, but it actually had a small bow at a French festival called the Angoulême Francophone Film Festival, where it won an Audience Award and a Special Prize for its cast. “The Daughters of Abraham” first opens in France on December 30. But Strand, a Culver City-based distributor behind recent releases like Mexico’s Oscar submission “On the Road,” “In a Whisper,” and the 4K restoration of Gregg Araki’s “Mysterious Skin,” will release it in North America in 2027.

“Honeymoon/Funeral”

Distributor: Black Bear
Director: Nahnatchka Khan
Festival: TIFF Market
Buzz: This market title is a rom-com starring an indelible trio of Greta Lee, Rebecca Ferguson, and Carrie Coon, and it wrapped production in September. Read more about the film here.

Films Acquired During the Festivals

“A Day in the Life of Jo: Chapter Phaedra”

Distributor: 1-2 Special
Director: Jacqueline Lentzou
Festival: Venice Orizzonti
Buzz: This Greek coming-of-age story won filmmaker Jacqueline Lentzou the Best Director prize in the Horizons section of the Venice Film Festival, but 1-2 Special picked it up after its North American premiere at NYFF and head of additional screenings at BFI London Film Festival, the Chicago International Film Festival, and the Busan International Film Festival. Blending what the release describes as both the “cosmic and the mundane,” the film follows a 15-year-old girl who meets a new classmate named Phaedra but also begins to notice signs and symbols from a dream world surfacing around her, ultimately leading her to an ethereal transformation. This is Lentzou’s second feature after 2021’s “Moon, 66 Questions.” 1-2 Special is planning a theatrical release for 2027.

“The Surgeon”

Distributor: Sony Pictures
Director: Roshan Sethi
Festival: TIFF Centrepiece
Buzz: This action-thriller starring Michelle Yeoh as a surgeon who is abducted and forced to operate on a mysterious patient is a bit of a departure for Sethi. Sethi’s previous film was the charming rom-com “A Nice Indian Boy,” and he’s also the co-creator of the medical drama “The Resident.” But reviews for the film were solid, and it’s not typical for the majors to buy festival titles, but Sony is already dating it for release on April 2, 2027.

Director: Joshua Giuliano

Buzz: IndieWire first broke the news about the film originally set up at the Independent Film Company and Shudder being picked up by Universal and Blumhouse Atomic Monster for a deal that could surpass $10 million as the companies hope to find the next “Obsession,” just as they did last year. Read more here.

The cast is stacked, including Issa Rae, Dan Stevens, Zach Cherry, Ed Helms, Ashley Park, Sharon Stone, and David Strathairn in supporting parts.

“Babies” is described as heartfelt and poignant in what is shaping up to be a strong year for Seth Rogen. The movie launched sales at TIFF nearly a year to the date prior to its Roy Thomson Hall premiere. The distributors are planning for a release in early 2027.

entry.title: ‘Avengers: Doomsday’ Has 10 Credited Writers, Including Hugh Jackman and Ryan Reynolds
entry.summary: 'Avengers: Doomsday' has ten credited screenwriters, including Hugh Jackman and Ryan Reynolds.
entry.content:
It appears that Marvel has assembled a team of earth’s mightiest screenwriters to shape its most epic blockbuster yet.

The Writer’s Guild of America has added the full list of writers who worked on “Avengers: Doomsday” to its directory, and comic book movie fans are already scanning it for clues about the film‘s contents. For one thing, the credits erase all doubts that Deadpool and Wolverine will appear in the film, as both Ryan Reynolds and Hugh Jackman are listed as providing additional literary material for the film. Reynolds was a writer on 2024’s Deadpool & Wolverine,” but this is actually Jackman’s first official writing credit listed in the WGA directory.

Related Stories
Brad Pitt to Star in ‘Connector’ from ‘Sound of Metal’ Director Darius Marder for Apple
‘American Doctor’ and ‘You Can See Everything’ Lead 2027 Cinema Eye Honors Film Nominations

When the credits finally roll at the end of the gargantuan superhero team-up, audience members will see that the screenplay was written by Marvel veterans Stephen McFeely and Michael Waldron. But the Guild’s database also lists writers who did behind-the-scenes work on the script. A whopping eight writers received that “additional literary material” credit: Reynolds, Jackman, Eric Pearson, Chris McKenna, Erik Sommers, Jeff Loveness, Andrew Lanham, and Destin Daniel Cretton.

The large list of writers is understandable when you consider how many characters “Doomsday” has to cover. In addition to catching audiences up with everyone who survived “Avengers: Endgame” (and in all likelihood, some people who didn’t thanks to the endless power of multiverses), the film also has to introduce Robert Downey Jr.’s Dr. Doom as the MCU’s new villain, integrate the characters from “Thunderbolts*” and “The Fantastic Four: First Steps,” and introduce the new X-Men that the studio hopes will become its next juggernaut superhero property. Many of the credited writers on “Doomsday” have recently written or directed those characters’ standalone films.

The writing credits also speak to the uniquely chaotic production process that the film employed. Joe and Anthony Russo, who returned to direct their first Marvel movie since “Endgame,” have publicly admitted to starting production without a finished script. Joe Russo recently told the Associated Press that they “always view the script as a living organism” that evolves throughout the shooting process. It’s unsurprising that such long shoot with a changing script and a revolving door of A-list actor schedules required the services of double digit writers along the way.

Disney will release “Avengers: Doomsday” in theaters on Friday, December 18.

entry.title: Saoirse Ronan Has Wanted to Direct Since She Was a Kid, and Her Exquisite First Short ‘Paper Plane’ Proves She’s Got the Goods
entry.summary: INTERVIEW: Saoirse Ronan has wanted to direct since she was a kid, and her deep-feeling and gorgeous short proves she's got the stuff.
entry.content:
Like all great directors, Saoirse Ronan has the multitasking thing down pat. Earlier this week, IndieWire exclusively spoke with Ronan as she was walking around London during a particularly “crazy busy” time in her life (yes, we asked about Sam Mendes’ Beatles films, and Ronan could only smile and note that she couldn’t share a thing about them at this moment). Headphones on, jacket collar up, Ronan was getting her steps in while also talking about something she’s wanted to do for a very long time: direct a film.

Earlier this month, Ronan’s “Paper Plane” won Best Narrative Short at the Austin Film Festival after debuting at Venice earlier in the season. Any win is nice, but a win at an Oscar-qualifying festival like Austin comes with an added sweetener: The film is instantly eligible for Oscar consideration for the 2027 ceremony. Jumping behind the camera is something Ronan has wanted to do for years, and her first offering (which she also wrote) is exquisite.

Related Stories
‘Avengers: Doomsday’ Has 10 Credited Writers, Including Hugh Jackman and Ryan Reynolds
Brad Pitt to Star in ‘Connector’ from ‘Sound of Metal’ Director Darius Marder for Apple

The 15-minute short film stars rising young actress Martha Malone as Fay, alongside Clare Dunne as Mam and Tim Creed as Dad. When we first meet Fay, she’s launched a silent protest, announcing to her mother (via a titular paper plane message) that she will not return to their home until her father, who we instantly understand is a toxic presence, leaves for good. As Fay and her trusty dog sit it out in a grassy lot across the street from the family home, Ronan’s film unfolds with grace and honesty, ending on a heart-stopping note.

Ronan also gathered an impressive roster behind the camera, including producer Shirin Eren, who previously produced Ronan’s “The Outrun,” IFTA-winning editor Nathan Nugent, and Kate McCullough, all of whom she describes in sparkling terms. You can get a taste of the film’s tone, visual style, and wonderful performances in an exclusive clip below.

Ahead, Ronan goes deep on her process, why she felt the need to make the jump to directing now (thanks to her “Little Women” co-star Eliza Scanlen), emulating her favorite collaborators like Greta Gerwig and Joe Wright, the one thing about directing that really surprised her, and if she’s ready to make the jump to directing features.

The following interview has been edited and condensed for clarity and length.

IndieWire: When we spoke in 2024 for “The Outrun,” you told me that you had wanted to direct since you were a child. Why was this the right project and the right moment?

Saoirse Ronan: I think it was a number of things. It was where I was at in my personal life. I was definitely starting to move into the next stage of adulthood. It felt like a shift was taking place for me internally. I was married, becoming a parent. Change was on the horizon.

And I think it felt, to be honest, if I don’t do it now, who knows when I’ll do it. I also wonder how many mothers in particular feel that way before they go into that next stage of their life where they’re like, “Actually, this is all quite unknown, and I don’t know if I don’t do it now, will it be another 10 years before I can find the time or the space within myself to do something like that that’s for me?” So it really gave me a lot of motivation being in that place personally.

It’s something that I’ve always wanted to do. I was always drawn toward directing, even from before I became an actor. And I’ve been so hugely influenced by the directors I’ve worked with since the age of 10. I guess I was ready to put that into action, and it was always going to be something that involved a young person and a mother, probably. It just felt very serendipitous that it happened when it did. So felt like everything was aligning at that point.

You also wrote this script. What was your writing process like? What surprised you about that?

Maybe it’s different with journalism, although I’m sure it must be incredibly difficult in other ways, but writing’s just really hard. And I knew it would be, but to conjure up something out of nothing supposedly is mind-boggling. I guess I didn’t realize how much of it is about process. As the Italians say, piano, piano, little by little, you take a step forward, and you take two steps back. I’d never been in that position creatively and professionally where it was all on me, so to find the discipline to do that, sit down, and to go, “OK, well, it’s not going to happen if I don’t make it happen,” was a new challenge for me.

I was so lucky to have Shirin Eren, my producer and my partner, Jack [Lowden], and lots of close friends who had already taken that step. Brilliant actor Eliza Scanlen, who’s already done three shorts, and she’s so much younger than I am, has actually been a huge inspiration to me. And I just thought, well, Jesus, if Eliza’s doing it, I have no excuse.

What I’ve learned is, when it comes to doing a feature, I’d definitely love to work with a writer, because I’m not one, and I think there’s a lot I have to learn. This was incredibly personal, so it was coming from such a pure place that it had to come from me, and it had to be written by me. But I certainly am excited by the challenge of working with someone who actually does it for a living and to learn about how to structure something and add art and things like that.

In the film’s press notes, it says that this is “a love letter to your younger self.” What was the most important thing that had to be in there for you, in terms of the script or the visuals or the casting?

There were two things that were very important to me. One was, tonally, I kept circling back to the magical realism route. I wanted it only ever to feel like we were seeing this through a child’s eyes, and in the way that a child makes sense out of the nonsensical and the seemingly impossible and the incredibly difficult thing to fathom and to swallow and to digest and to overcome. Creativity and imagination always plays a part for a child and just making sense out of anything in the world from day dot, from the moment that they’re here. I didn’t want it to feel like a fantasy, but I wanted it to feel like it was heightened in some way, hence the addition of the paper planes, which was something I used to do with my mom.

I used to send her little paper planes when she’d send me to my room with a little note saying, “I’m really sorry that I did this. Please don’t hate me. Please don’t send me back,” or whatever. And I’d peek around the corner of whatever room she was in, I’d throw it at her, and then I’d run back to my room knowing logically she’d know it was me, but tricking myself into believing that she’d believed that this had seemingly come out of nowhere.

It was also very important to me that the father role was never vilified. I didn’t want this to be a piece that was overly black and white and critical when it comes to the situation. I didn’t want to just point the blame at one character. Although there’s clearly something very toxic and dark within the home that’s happening, and it’s ultimately being created by one member of the family for the most part, there’s a reason why this person unfortunately feels the need within themselves to create that toxicity.

I never wanted it to feel like there was any hatred or anger toward that character. It needed to very much be focused on the love of these two girls. Becoming a mother, I really felt with myself that you don’t ever stop being a child. You can say that we become more sophisticated, but I actually don’t know how much we do. And I think to have a character that’s an older female, an older person, and someone who’s younger, but who essentially both remind each other of their inner child, I wanted to bring that out too.

You’ve worked with so many incredible filmmakers over the course of your career. Was there any filmmaker you really wanted to emulate in terms of how you ran your set?

Oh gosh, how I ran my set! It’s a combination of a few people. I think back in the day, the way Joe Wright ran his set was fantastic. The way he was on the ground with his crew, the clarity that he had at the top of the day, the structure he had when it came to planning, I’ve always responded really well to that. I think I was really influenced by that from working with him so early on. The fact that he and Peter Jackson as well always played music live on set, I’ve always felt like that’s a really helpful way to remind cast and crew that, yes, there’s emotional truth in this, but for me, I want to make movies, I want to make films. They’re not documentaries, so there needs to be this heightened quality to it. I feel like having music on set can remind people of that and just get everyone on the same rhythm.

I think the way Greta [Gerwig] is just Greta and John Crowley, the way they are as directors with their actors, I haven’t marched with anyone greater than those two. They bring out something that I haven’t experienced with anyone else, really, and I’ll always strive to be a tenth to what they are as a director. One thing that Greta said is that you need to think of yourself as the most supportive audience member for your actors. She always makes you feel so loved and interesting and wanted, and so I wanted the actors to feel that way.

And to be honest, weirdly, out of every kind of hat that I had to wear as director, directing the actors was the thing that made me the most nervous. Everything else, I was all right, but it felt really natural. But to actually be in the driving seat with other actors and to guide them, I was really, really nervous about that and constantly feeling like, God, I can’t let them down. I can’t steer them wrong. I always want them to feel safe, and they can do whatever they want to do.

Was that the most surprising thing for you?

Yes, that really did surprise me. I wasn’t expecting that, but actually when I think about it and when I think about the kind of actor that I am, it does make sense, because I’m not one of those actors ever that’s like, “Don’t worry, I’ll take control of the room.” Maybe I’ve started to do that more as I’ve gotten older, but we all know plenty of actors that will start giving other actors notes, which is never helpful. Well, sometimes it is actually, maybe that’s not true, but I haven’t been that kind of actor. So that definitely took me by surprise just how self-conscious I was initially. But I think they were happy. The girls said that they felt good, so that’s all I can ask for really.

In our interview for “The Outrun,” we talked about process, and your process is so internal and personal. It’s about being in the moment. You’re not Method. You don’t get caught up in stuff, so I did wonder how that would translate to directing.

It was funny actually because that seemed to translate well. I think because of the way I work, it’s so much about working with the crew and enjoying the atmosphere on set, and it feels so natural for me to be there, so I felt really confident doing that. I’ve been on so many sets where I’ve looked at directors or producers who don’t quite know how to talk to their crew, don’t quite know what the crew needs, and how to wrangle the truth, how to make them feel appreciated and motivated. I feel like I know how to do that. I’ve been on so many sets and grown up with it, and more than anyone else, I spend time with the crew, and I hear what irks them, what their complaints are, what drives them forward, what they appreciate from a director, from a leader.

So I knew what to do in that sense, I think, I hope. I loved working with my first AD. I loved working on the schedule with her. I loved being able to work so in-depth with a production designer. Actors never get to do that kind of stuff. I don’t think being a director is necessarily the hardest job out of every crew member. I think that the skill of being a director is to surround yourself with really, really, really brilliant people who know what they’re doing and to have good taste.

Watch an exclusive clip from “Paper Plane” below.

It sounds like it was pretty joyous for you to assemble your crew.

I think what every director will tell you, which I now know, is that making a short film is fucking really hard and frustrating, because crew need to go and work on a film that will actually pay the money and will keep them employed for two, three months, and a short film is not going to do that.

So actually being able to get the crew that you want can be really, really difficult, but it does mean that the people who do come on board are there because they really want to be. It’s not because they’re getting paid. It’s not because it’s necessarily going to further their career or anything like that. It’s just, they’re doing it because they want it, because they love what they do, and they want to get their energy in the story. They were there because they wanted to invest themselves in the story, and they also wanted to support me, which was just so lovely.

You’re someone who started acting at a young age, so I find it very interesting and compelling that you centered your film around a young star. How did you make sure Martha felt safe and comfortable and supported?

I knew that on day one, Martha was going to be super nervous. She was 14, 15 at the time, and she’d done a few things, but I think whenever any of us have our first day on set, no matter how experienced we are, we’re always scared. I just wanted her to know that I was too, that I was nervous as well, and that we were going to be nervous together, and it was OK, and we were going to take care of each other.

I have the utmost respect for young performers, and I think that when you find ones that are disciplined as well as being talented, you just need to make them feel like they’re never pressured, they’re supported, but they’re being pushed. You’re not necessarily wrapping them in cotton wool, but you want them to feel loved. I wanted her and Claire to feel loved and wanted because they were, and that ultimately I would have to guide us because somebody does, but that there was a contribution they were going to be able to make as performers that I couldn’t, and I valued that.

You mentioned if you make a feature, you want to work with another writer. The inevitable question: Do you want to direct a feature?

Yeah, I do. I do want to do a feature, and I think part of the reason why I was making shorts is because I wanted to see if I could, and if I could, then what was my style, and what did I respond to, and what did I need to work on, and what were my strengths, so that I didn’t use everyone as my training ground on a feature film.

Again, I’ve been on the other side of that as well, where you’ve got someone in the driving seat, and you’re like, “Uh-oh.” I didn’t want to put anyone else in that position. I didn’t want to put myself in that position. I loved it so much, and I do have a lot to learn. I really want to keep going with it. So I would love to do a feature. I have a rough idea of what I want to do, but I know now that that can be the starting point and that it will become what it’s meant to become.

entry.title: Brad Pitt to Star in ‘Connector’ from ‘Sound of Metal’ Director Darius Marder for Apple
entry.summary: Brad Pitt is starring in a film from 'Sound of Metal' director Darius Marder called 'Connector' that has been acquired by Apple.
entry.content:
Brad Pitt is reuniting with Apple after making “F1” together, this time teaming with “Sound of Metal” director Darius Marder on a ’70s period drama.

Apple Original Films has acquired the rights to “Connector,” which will be directed by and co-written by Marder along with his sibling Nina Marder. Pitt and the Marders will also be producing the film via his Plan B banner, and Apple will serve as the studio.

After making his debut with “Sound of Metal,” which dealt with heavy metal music, Marder is now getting into literal heavy metals. “Connector” stars Pitt as a sky-walking ironworker in 1970s New York City who becomes a working class legend and takes on forces larger than himself, per the logline.

Related Stories
‘American Doctor’ and ‘You Can See Everything’ Lead 2027 Cinema Eye Honors Film Nominations
What Makes a Good Oscar Campaign? Just Ask Sony Classics’ Michael Barker and Tom Bernard

Marder’s directorial debut was “Sound of Metal” from 2019, which starred Riz Ahmed as a drummer who goes deaf after years of playing. The film was a boon for deaf representation and earned six Oscar nominations, including Best Picture and Best Original Screenplay, also winning two for Best Sound and Best Film Editing. “Connector” is his follow-up project. He also previously co-wrote Derek Cianfrance’s drama “The Place Beyond the Pines.”

Pitt this year starred in “Heart of the Beast” and will next be seen in “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth,” David Fincher’s pseudo-sequel that sees Pitt reprise his Oscar-winning role from “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood.” “F1” was a major hit for Apple, one of the few movies it actually still released in theaters (partnering with Warner Bros.) and gave a robust theatrical window before ultimately releasing it on Apple TV. The film made $634.1 million worldwide at the box office.

This is also the third collaboration between Plan B and Apple after “F1,” the other being the recently announced “The Waffle House Index,” which will star “Obsession” breakout Inde Navarette.

Deadline first reported on the news.

entry.title: ‘American Doctor’ and ‘You Can See Everything’ Lead 2027 Cinema Eye Honors Film Nominations
entry.summary: 'American Doctor' and 'You Can See Everything' lead the 2027 Cinema Eye Honors film nominations with seven nods each.
entry.content:
The Cinema Eye Honors have revealed nominations for the 20th annual awards ceremony. Leading the pack are Po Si Teng’s “American Doctor” and Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s “You Can See Everything” with seven nominations each.

The A24 Elizabeth Holmes movie also made Cinema Eye Honors history as the first film to be nominated for Nonfiction Feature, Direction, Editing, Production, Cinematography, and Original Score — along with the Audience Choice Prize.

Other films that fared well in nominations for the ceremony honoring outstanding artistic achievement in nonfiction and documentary films and series, which is often a bellwether for the Best Documentary Feature Oscar race, are Sara Dosa’s “Time and Water,” which scored six nominations, and recent Neon acquisition “NAZA,” which earned five nominations. Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, directors of the latter film, won at the 2025 Cinema Eye Honors for their previous film “No Other Land,” which won the Oscar for Best Documentary Feature.

Related Stories
What Makes a Good Oscar Campaign? Just Ask Sony Classics’ Michael Barker and Tom Bernard
‘Ebenezer’ Review: Johnny Depp Is Absolutely Insufferable in a Dull and Dreary Christmas Carol

For individual recognition, “American Doctor” filmmaker Po Si Teng has the most nominations this year, with five. “You Can See Everything” directors Fielder and Oppenheim received four apiece. Meanwhile, documentarian Jimmy Chin, who earned three nominations for “Everest: The Other Side,” which he co-directed with Elizabeth Chai Vasarhelyi, moves into third on the all-time nominations list with 14 total nods.

Among distributors, HBO, National Geographic and Netflix tied with the most nominations, with each receiving 12 nods across all categories. Neon followed with nine nominations, while A24 and Watermelon Pictures both had seven.

After a first round of voting that saw nonfiction fans worldwide cast tens of thousands of votes for their favorite films, the Audience Choice nominees were announced. The last eight winners of the Best Documentary Feature Oscar— “Mr. Nobody Against Putin,” “No Other Land,” “20 Days in Mariupol,” “Navalny,” “Summer of Soul,” “My Octopus Teacher,” “American Factory,” and “Free Solo”— were all first contenders for the Audience Choice Prize. Second-round voting to determine this year’s winner will take place in December.

In addition to the previously announced Unforgettables Honorees, Broadcast nominees, and the Shorts List, Cinema Eye announced that Steve James’ documentary masterpiece, “Hoop Dreams,” will receive this year’s Legacy Award, presented to a classic nonfiction film that continues to inspire today’s working filmmakers.

This season, Cinema Eye will return to the Times Center in New York City, the home of its second and third editions, for its 20th Awards Ceremony on Monday, January 11, 2027. Cinema Eye Week, which includes events and activities for Cinema Eye nominees and honorees, kicks off in New York on Friday, January 8.

entry.title: What Makes a Good Oscar Campaign? Just Ask Sony Classics’ Michael Barker and Tom Bernard
entry.summary: The Sony Pictures Classics co-presidents join IndieWire's 'Screen Talk' podcast to talk 2027 Oscars and more.
entry.content:
Sony Pictures Classics co-presidents Michael Barker and Tom Bernard have been the white whale of IndieWire’s “Screen Talk” podcast for years. Finally, they joined us for an engaging chat about the specialty label’s robust slate of films this year — and about Oscar campaigning and developments in the business.

Together, Barker and Bernard have reigned over the theatrical specialty universe for decades, believing in the theatrical model all along. And it seems to be roaring back, with a three-hour documentary at number two at the box office, and a foreign-language “Godzilla” movie at number one. Black Bear’s indie “Wicker” is in the top 10 and, earlier this fall, Sony Pictures Classics’ Sundance indie “The Only Living Pickpocket in New York,” starring Oscar hopeful John Turturro, was in the top 10.

Related Stories
‘Ebenezer’ Review: Johnny Depp Is Absolutely Insufferable in a Dull and Dreary Christmas Carol
Sandra Wollner’s ‘Everytime’ Is a Stunning Film About Grief Like You’ve Never Seen Before

In this week’s podcast, Barker and Bernard talk about films including Pedro Almodóvar’s “Bitter Christmas”; Florian Zeller’s critically divisive but audience-appreciated “Bunker”; and the UK’s international Oscar entry from Iran, “Rehearsals for a Revolution,” which is also vying for Best Documentary Feature. They’re also backing the animated “Iron Boy” this year, plus Sundance winner “Bedford Park.” They also tease “Violette,” their latest acquisition, and the new film from “Amélie” director Jean-Pierre Jeunet.

Elsewhere on the podcast, we also mourn the unexpected passing of Chilean filmmaker Sebastian Lélio, dissect Letterboxd’s sales to The New York Times, and the dismissal of James Gunn and Peter Safran from DC Studios.

Plus, co-hosts Anne Thompson and Ryan Lattanzio strongly encourage audiences to see Kelly O’Sullivan and Alex Thompson’s excellent indie “Mouse” as it expands nationwide this weekend. Sophie Okonedo is hugely deserving of best supporting actress accolades, but the film needs critics to continue advocating for it.
