entry.title: ‘Ebenezer’ Review: Johnny Depp Is Absolutely Insufferable in a Dull and Dreary Christmas Carol
entry.summary: Ti West's horror-inflected 'Ebenezer' has a few nice flourishes, but Depp's muggy performance torpedoes the whole thing from the start. Review.
entry.content:
A Sauvage and jowly overactor in dire need of career rehabilitation could hardly ask for a better part to play than Ebenezer Scrooge. He’s a cruel miser of a man who comes to learn the error of his ways over the course of a ghost story that preys upon Christian precepts of redemption and forgiveness (along with the more secular warm and fuzzies of seeing a bad guy discover the joys of being good). Indeed, what is “cancel culture” if not a shackled delusion that visits self-made pariahs in the dead of night, and what is Charles Dickens’ “A Christmas Carol” if not a plea to believe that even the most odious of souls are still capable of being saved?

Related Stories
Sandra Wollner’s ‘Everytime’ Is a Stunning Film About Grief Like You’ve Never Seen Before
How ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Dominated the Box Office: GKIDS Chief on IMAX’s Impact and the Growing Market for Foreign-Language Movies

It’s been reported that Johnny Depp accepted the title role of Ti West’s “Ebenezer” at a fraction of his usual rate, but I suspect that he probably would have done this movie for free. While the embattled star earned more than $250 million for his work on the “Pirates of the Caribbean” franchise, even that psychotic number pales in comparison to the pricelessness of starring in a major studio Christmas movie that allows him to look just left of the camera and say lines like “I’m not the man I was!” and “I was once good, and I know I can be again!” before his character saves a cherubic little boy from certain death and invites a freezing beggar inside for a warm cup of tea. If an old crank like Scrooge can make his way back toward grace, why not the convicted star of “Mortdecai,” and the alleged perpetrator of several even more serious crimes?

Johnny Depp may prefer for that to be framed as a rhetorical question, but his insufferable turn as literature’s most cantankerous moneylender demands an honest answer. For me, that answer is rather straightforward: While Depp has never been the subtlest of actors, his post-Sparrow pivot away from artistic curiosity has distended his talents into such a grotesque caricature of their former charm that “Ebenezer” left me feeling like I may never be able to empathize with his screen presence again.

Scrooge is obviously a scenery-chewer’s dream, but the crescent arc he traces from grinch to Christmas miracle is only believable enough to sustain Dickens’ fable if you believe it on both ends. Depp’s performance — an advent calendar of empty affectations without a soul to anchor them, every shot full of face and bereft of feeling — makes that exceedingly difficult. His offscreen unsavoriness certainly doesn’t help, but there’s a more immediate problem when the lights go down, one that makes him a unique case among Hollywood’s tainted array of mega-star actors: He seems to have become very bad at acting. Whatever my feelings about Depp as a human being, the truth is that I didn’t buy him as a glowering monster any more than I bought him as a beaming man who’s grown “better than his word.”

An unengaging Ebenezer is a tough break for a movie called “Ebenezer,” and screenwriter Nathaniel Halpern’s fidelity to the source material doesn’t exactly leave West with a wealth of opportunities to compensate for such fatal miscasting. West’s take on the holiday classic is faithful to the core — no Muppets, no ghosts of girlfriends past, no uncanny mo-capped Jim Carrey. As you might expect from the director of indie genre standouts like “Pearl” and “The House of the Devil,” West’s big idea is to scare the Dickens out of us by turning up the volume on this story’s implicit scariness. Sometimes literally, as this PG-13 carol offers a small handful of gentle jump-scares.

“Ebenezer” isn’t a horror movie in the strictest sense, but West does what he can to play up the fear that eventually terrifies Scrooge into giving a shit about his fellow man. Most — or all — of those flourishes are purely cosmetic in nature, and hellbent on sucking every glimmer of life out of Victorian England. Scrooge’s office has never looked more haunted, as Checco Varese’s grimdark cinematography and Eve Stewart’s Yharnam-esque production design combine to create a London that’s in dire need of Christmas cheer (the vibe should go a long way with tweenage audiences eager for a bit of spice with their holiday viewing, though I suspect the whole thing is too staid and oppressive to become any kind of perennial favorite).

And since West would sooner die than pass up a chance for death, this version of the story treats us to a musty prologue where we actually get to see Ebenezer’s business partner bite the dust with his mouth wide open (Marley is played by Ian McKellen in what currently stands as the most “remember ‘The Christophers?’” performance of the year). From there, the action skips forward to Christmas Eve 1843, whence Ebenezer is inflicting his usual “Bah, humbug!” routine on poor Bob Cratchit (Rupert Grint), the underpaid clerk he resents for taking the next day off (HR being a decidedly 20th-century invention). But the fates have plans of their own for the bitter-cold businessman, who promptly pisses himself when the ghost of old Marley bursts into his miserable bedchamber later that night.

Reaction shots ensue, as Depp curdles his face into a series of the most exaggerated expressions since the death of silent cinema, every one of them betraying his character’s frigidness. This Ebenezer takes an active pleasure in being cruel, which not only makes him more detestable (which is fine), but also endows him with an innate capacity for joy that makes the rest of the movie feel like it’s walking in circles (which is less fine). Given that Depp’s performance is only as wide as his lips and as deep as his pockets, it seems wasteful that we should have to walk through the hollows of Ebenezer’s past, present, and future in order to fix him — it would be easier and equally meaningful to just push the corners of his mouth into a smile.

Of course, that would deprive us of the “holy shit, that’s Andrea Riseborough” fun of the “To Leslie” star’s Ghost of Christmas Past, a white-eyed ghoul who looks like a spirit from “The Conjuring” who popped up for a sudden jolt and then forgot to leave the frame. She’s the most amusing part of a familiar tour through the sadness of Ebenezer’s childhood, where he was bullied by the other kids and kept apart from his beloved older sister. Tramell Tillman is equally compelling as the boisterous Ghost of Christmas Present, though his bizarre character design — a round-bellied man whose face appears to be rotting to pieces in real-time — turns out to be reverse-engineered from an unnerving reveal that both honors Dickens’ text and also underlines West’s limited conviction to rejuvenate it with the visceral immediacy of a horror film (his commitment to the bit falls well short of the Robert Eggers-level follow-through that conceit demands).

Given the emphasis the director puts on the film’s genre spin, it’s ironic and surprising that “Ebenezer” is at its best when it focuses on the most basic human elements of its story, if only because the supporting characters offer such a welcome contrast to whatever Depp is doing. Sam Claflin and Daisy Ridley don’t have a whole lot to do as Ebenezer’s kind-hearted nephew Fred and his wife Clara (respectively), but the film takes pains to stress how sad it is that Scrooge is Fred’s last connection to his dead mother, and it’s touching to see how much it would mean for him to have a cordial relationship with the old miser.

It is considerably less touching to see Ebenezer arrive at a mutual feeling after palling around with the film’s Nazgûl-coded Ghost of Christmas Yet to Come (Robert Strange, cloaked in CGI), who forces the misanthrope to face the emptiness of his own miserable existence. “The flame of humanity still flickers within you,” someone tells Scrooge, but the slapstick pageantry of Depp’s performance sabotages the movie by keeping that flame at a low simmer from the start. I didn’t believe the fire had ever gone out any more than I believed that it was eventually rekindled, as this Ebenezer Scrooge is far too elastic and self-amused to convincingly suggest that he’s experiencing a permanent change of heart. He can’t even sustain a facial expression for more than a few seconds before he starts mugging around in search of another one.

There will, of course, be those who insist that I only panned “Ebenezer” because Johnny Depp is in it, and I suppose they’re at least half-right about that, if not quite for the reason they assume. The truth is that it would be a lot more interesting and true to the spirit of Dickens’ classic if I liked this movie in spite of Depp rather than disliking it because of him, as I can’t help but share the author’s opinion that everyone is theoretically capable of redemption, be it measure by measure or miraculously complete.

Alas, the actor’s “comeback” performance is just yet another thing that he ought to be sorry for.

Grade: C-

Paramount Pictures will release “Ebenezer” in theaters on Friday, November 13.

entry.title: After ‘Whalefall’ Flops, Can Imagine Entertainment Return to Box Office Glory with ‘How to Rob a Bank’?
entry.summary: After "Whalefall" bombed, Ron Howard and Brian Grazer's Imagine Entertainment is still looking for theatrical hits with "Spaceballs" and "How to Rob a Bank."
entry.content:
“How to Rob a Bank” may benefit from doing just that. With career-low reviews for director David Leitch, the Amazon MGM Studios release has been tracking poorly and now looks unlikely to crack $10 million from 2,810 theaters in its domestic debut.

For the film’s production banner, Imagine Entertainment, it is shaping up to be a second theatrical non-starter after its high-concept survival thriller “Whalefall” — about a scuba diver trapped in the belly of a marine mammal — got beached after its October opening with just a $39 million total worldwide despite solid reviews. Neither “How to Rob a Bank” nor “Whalefall” marks an auspicious wide release homecoming for Imagine, even if Amazon and Disney, respectively, fronted the budget and marketing spend on the films.

Related Stories
‘How to Rob a Bank’ Review: David Leitch’s Fun and Poppy YouTube Heist Movie Almost Gets Away with It
Ebenezer’s Venmo and ‘How to Rob a Bank’ ATMs: Studios Are Now Promoting Movies by Just Giving Away Money

The two features are Imagine’s first to play across more than 2,000 domestic screens in more than eight years; the last was Lionsgate’s buddy comedy “The Spy Who Dumped Me” in 2018. That’s practically an epoch for Imagine, which was founded by Ron Howard and Brian Grazer and spent its early years asserting itself as a theatrical force with hits like “Kindergarten Cop,” “Liar, Liar,” “The Nutty Professor,” and Howard’s own films, like “Apollo 13” and “How the Grinch Stole Christmas.” A spokesperson for the banner declined to comment for this report.

But Imagine, as with much of the industry, saw its focus on original, often adult-oriented programming hit diminishing returns in the past 20 years. The company’s biggest hit after 2010 was the 2016 Dan Brown adaptation “Inferno,” which, at $220 million global, earned less than half the gross that its 2009 predecessor “Angels & Demons” did.

Around that time, Imagine hitched its wagon to the then-burgeoning streaming industry, expanding its focus on television projects and aggressively branching into the documentary market, as theatrical features fell by the wayside. Packages for narrative features like “Tick, Tick… Boom!” and “The Beanie Bubble” were sold off to streaming services. But with an industrywide reawakening to the benefits of theatrical (which has even drawn in Netflix), along with a waning demand for unscripted programming, Imagine is now at the start of its return to wide-release, big-screen features.

There were some false starts along the way. Notably, Howard’s own 2022 rescue thriller “Thirteen Lives” had originally been set up at MGM before the studio’s acquisition by Amazon, which then executed an extremely limited theatrical release and opted out of reporting box office. The film’s star Viggo Mortensen later slammed the decision. Then there was Howard’s island-set thriller “Eden,” which sold to the mostly digital-focused distributor Vertical after debuting to withering reviews. And Luca Guadagnino’s post-#MeToo morality thriller “After the Hunt” never cracked 1,300 theaters from Amazon MGM after critics ripped it apart at Venice Film Festival. Many of these films carried hefty price tags — “Eden” had a $35 million net budget, while “After the Hunt” cost $80 million to produce.

“How to Rob a Bank,” co-produced by director Leitch’s 87North, faces a significant climb to any theatrical success with a $40 million production budget and intense Thanksgiving season competition incoming. Imagine has a more promising (though less novel) plan to lean further into IP in 2027. Another Amazon MGM release, the legacy sequel comedy “Spaceballs: The New One,” will come in April. And Universal is distributing a Snoop Dogg biopic, which Imagine developed along with the rapper’s own Death Row Pictures. Can Imagine find the same success with Snoop’s story that it did with “8 Mile”?

More original is the Adam Driver military thriller “Alone at Dawn,” directed by Howard himself, which shot in 2025 and is slated for a Christmas 2027 theatrical release from Amazon MGM. Further down the line, Imagine is developing a sequel to “How the Grinch Stole Christmas,” with Jim Carrey tapped to return. The first film was the top-grossing North American release of 2000 and remains a high watermark for Imagine’s commercial success.

Imagine Entertainment’s future of theatrical IP also comes after years of murmurs that the banner was fielding suitors amid its rise in the documentary space, including a Variety report of a 2021 valuation around $800 million and a 2022 report from TheWrap that a $700 million valuation deal with Centricus Asset Management Ltd. had fallen through. But more recently, TheWrap reported on October 1 that majority stakeholder The Raine Group, which came aboard for $100 million in 2016, was in talks to sell its 51 percent ownership to private equity; an Imagine representative issued an emphatic denial of the claim in the piece.

After a boom among independent production banners to start the decade, the business has faced growing instability over recent years, with shrinking valuations and sharp cutbacks in content spending. For decades, Imagine has been one of the industry leaders in the space, but “How to Rob a Bank” and “Whalefall” are the first test of whether it can reassert itself as a theatrical hitmaker. If the poor tracking for “Rob a Bank” pans out, it’ll then look to “Spaceballs” for, as the joke in Mel Brooks’ 1987 goes, “The Search for More Money.”

entry.title: Sandra Wollner’s ‘Everytime’ Is a Stunning Film About Grief Like You’ve Never Seen Before
entry.summary: Sandra Wollner's 'Everytime' is filled with the unexpected. She tells IndieWire about video games, that tragic fall, and what it all means. Sort of.
entry.content:
Few human emotions are as fathomable as grief. Someone (or something) was here, had meaning and value and presence, and is now gone. There is a hole, a gap, an empty space. The pain that accompanies that void may manifest in different people in different ways, but its very existence is understandable. What makes people happy? What makes them sad? What makes them angry? Grief, well, that’s an easier question with a tougher answer.

For her third feature film, German filmmaker Sandra Wollner tackles the most tangible of dramatic genres — the grief tale — and turns it on its head in a way that our own David Ehrlich called “infinitely beguiling.” Mostly, the film shows how infinitely elastic and malleable this genre is, and the emotions that power it.

Related Stories
How ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Dominated the Box Office: GKIDS Chief on IMAX’s Impact and the Growing Market for Foreign-Language Movies
Democrats Won. When Do Hollywood Crews Get Back to Work?

The logline for the Un Certain Regard winner is simple enough: after the death of teenager Jessie (Carla Hüttermann), her mother Ella (Birgit Minichmayr), her little sister Melli (Lotte Shirin Keiling), and her boyfriend Lux (Tristán López) form an unlikely family unit as they attempt to move on. To say much else is spoiler-y in the truest of senses: It would detract from the joy and wonder of watching this story unfold.

That Wollner’s film is doing something different with seemingly well-trod material is obvious from the start, as “Everytime” layers on cut scenes from the video game “Vintage Story” — not “Minecraft,” though Wollner understands why the audience might think it’s the more well-known game — long before the real drama kicks in.

A familiarity with “Vintage Story” is not required to understand her film, Wollner promised during a recent interview with IndieWire. “Maybe if someone hears the dialogue of Melli and Lux, then maybe they would feel they have to know more about it, because they’re talking about how you can basically cut trees to harvest stuff and to get that, but I don’t feel that you have to know anything,” she said.

Wollner herself isn’t even a “hardcore gamer,” but she admires video games for their world-building and how they can encourage exploration. Her early forays into both “Vintage Story” and “Minecraft” tickled that. “It felt like the ‘Backrooms’ phenomenon, but before the ‘Backrooms’ phenomenon,” she said. “You’re walking through infinite worlds that feel so big, but minimalistic in a way. And the sounds; a very ambient sound feels eerie and soothing at the same time. I was just very compelled and inspired by that.”

The idea that Jessie would leave behind her own video game world that Melli could then play in was one of the film’s first seeds. “I thought, it’s a way of a memorial I haven’t seen so far,” she said. “[We have this] whole world of avatars and gaming communities where people meet online and then if someone really goes out, their avatar might live forever in there and create a life on its own in a way. I just found that very intriguing, and this is why I wanted in there.”

While the film is unique in how it handles digital mementos — avatars, literally — Wollner also pays close attention to real-world details that can make grief feel even bigger.

“One of the first scenes [I thought of] was Ella lying down on the couch and hearing how her daughter would come back [into their apartment],” the filmmaker said. “It’s something I think also everybody can relate to, even with a more natural loss and not such a tragic one. For example, when I was a kid, my aunt would always run down the stairs [in the apartment complex where we lived], and I would always hear her in the morning, running down in the morning. The noise was very specific to this person. I didn’t want it to be full on, but to let us think, it couldn’t be Jessie.”

Wollner was also intrigued early on by the “constellation of people” impacted by the loss of one. “The boy, the little girl, and the mother, it’s people I’ve met in my life in several decades, I would say, variations of them, but somehow similar constellations,” she said. “They seemed very clear to me. Three people who, especially the mother and the boy, really tried to do the right thing in a way. But there is a big conflict in there. They are having a weird dependent relationship. She needs him to grieve. He needs her to forgive. Of course, I could have made this conflict much bigger, but I really was interested in ordinary people who just try to do the right thing and just try to go along with that.”

Having her own child added a new dimension to the film, even for Wollner. The filmmaker was editing the film when her daughter was born (her longtime partner is writer and cinematographer Timm Kröger, who also worked on the digital imaging in “Everytime”), an experience that deepened her understanding of her own work.

In the film’s second half, the trio travel to Tenerife, Spain on holiday, a place that baby Jessie (who we’ve seen in home videos) once visited. There, they discover another baby, who looks just like Jessie, playing happily in the same quiet space that baby Jessie once occupied.

“We watched the scene again of baby Jessie sitting there, and we looked at each other,” she said. “I always understood what [that scene] means for me, but there, we really felt it for the first time, being a parent. And I felt, oh, I really nailed it! I mean, that sounds so stupid, but when I had the baby, I think, as many people feel, you still sometimes have the feeling, oh, where does it come from? It’s suddenly here. Suddenly there’s a person there. It’s like with that moment when she walks around the corner, and baby’s sitting there.”

Wollner was also compelled by the way we memorize different places and the unpredictability of memory. The odd little space, located in the far reaches of the resort’s clubhouse, comes to haunt Ella, Melli, and Lux in different ways, forever linked to Jessie and her absence.

“When my dad died, I was with him, and I suddenly had this image of him standing somewhere in this bend on the river and fishing, and it felt so familiar,” the filmmaker said. “This memory intruded on my present. We cannot control when we get a memory. They’re just coming. Sometimes we can make them happen to come. But we never know if maybe the weird place where we saw our baby sitting or the weird moment is the one that haunts us the most. It’s this weird banal little room with this weird banal kitschy toy that is playing this music. And this is the thing that then comes back.”

Those “banal little” details pack immense emotional power. So do turns from Minichmayr and López, who never turn to over-the-top histrionics to convey their grief. Wollner’s choice to set the majority of the film a year after Jessie’s death helped, giving the characters some distance from the immediate stab of loss.

“It was a conscious choice to pick some time after the death [to mostly focus the film on],” she said. “As a writer, we need to know what happened in the time between, and so I wrote that as well, but it honestly felt not depictable. I feel I can only fail to show that. I wasn’t interested in these big emotions. That just felt too overwhelming. And sometimes we are made to believe that grief comes in these neat boxes to check: Now you’re sad, now you’re angry, now you accept. Maybe you can be angry again, then you accept. It’s just this messy thing that you can feel for a very long time.”

Keiling also offers a nuanced performance, built more on a kid’s curiosity than on saddling the young actress with big, showy scenes. There’s no screaming and crying here, no sobbing or yelling. But that doesn’t mean that Keiling wasn’t accessing some major emotions.

“I love to work with kids,” Wollner said. “And even having a kid, I think I still am a kid in a way. For this one, I met Lotte, I had not met another kid, I only met her, I did not do any other castings. I just fell in love and thought, oh, she’s exactly what I thought of Melli could be and even better, so I trusted the script to her.”

Wollner worked with fellow filmmaker Juli Neuhaus, who served as a “kids’ coach” for the younger members of the cast. Wollner and Neuhaus were eager to meet Keiling where she was. The young performer loves to draw, so she would draw the scenes before performing them, to better understand what they were about, which allowed her to access a full spectrum of feeling.

“With Melli, there was no scene where she really had to act her grief,” she said. “I always felt that the film itself, the editing and the framing, the absence, we see her doing her homework, and then we see the same room behind her, but now we know that the sister is not there anymore, I always felt that this will tell us the grief, so she doesn’t need to act it. If she holds her phone and is texting her sister, it will already make us feel the grief. She doesn’t need to feel the heavy weight of that. So, actually for her, it was, I would say, like a very light shoot. Playful. It was really playful.”

Still, for all its sense of fantasy and play, “Everytime” is about a terrible heartbreak. Yet, as ever, Wollner chose to depict Jessie’s sudden, shocking death in a unique way, tracking her fall from a tall building while out with Lux from a great distance away. We can see it. We can do nothing about it. That’s grief, too.

“This was one that really was clear to me in the writing process already, that we’re going to have this lens and that we have this weird perspective of the universe itself looking at it, being so far away and still not able to do something about it, but still witnessing so intimate,” she said.

The actors were on one high-rise building, while Wollner and her crew were on another, about half a mile away. “And we had this insane lens. I had a 3,000-millimeter consumer camera, which is an insane lens,” she said. “It’s really like you don’t want to point it on people. It feels really not OK. But I was sure that I wanted to work with exactly that length or something similar to that, that feels kind of forbidden to be so close and too far away at the same time.”

While the scene is shot as if Jessie and Lux are very close to the edge of the building, the actors were not. (Hüttermann later told Wollner that she still had the feeling she might fall, even with myriad safety measures in place. That’s just how immersive the entire thing felt.) Hüttermann’s actual fall was shot in a studio, and their visual effects supervisor Kariem Saleh combined that footage with the outdoor shots.

Because they needed a certain kind of light, Wollner estimated they had only about five takes to get it right, though she knew they would likely only get one shot with the “perfect” light. Her script also called for the camera to follow a bird after the fall, but she said with a laugh, “Unfortunately, no bird came in exactly that moment.” (They lensed other birds, though, and those also ended up in the final composite shot.)

“We worked so many hours just on the sounds, just to get the right level of there is a little sound, and there is a little tink when she falls down, a little bit,” she said. “Just to realize, given how far away we had to be, how does the sound have to be? We worked the whole time on that, and I never really felt it until I sat at Cannes in the audience. And I heard the gasps for the first time and really it went through my bones. I mean, it’s weird to say that, but I was happy, but I felt the first time that it actually worked.”

Wollner remains very emotionally connected to the film, constantly talking about the way certain scenes make her feel, either while making them or editing them or even seeing them with an audience. Of course, such a deep-feeling filmmaker crafted such a beguiling film, one that invites all sorts of responses and theories. Since Cannes, audiences have been talking about its genuinely thrilling third act and the implications of its final scenes. And while we won’t spoil them here, we had to ask: What did Wollner want her viewers to feel in those moments?

“The feeling that I wanted to have is that [this film that is] grounded or hopefully grounded in the beginning, then suddenly you walk around the corner and you feel still some ground, but it’s such an odd place now and you don’t know,” she said. “I always hoped it doesn’t feel just dreamy, but there is some groundedness to it and that the people still react in a way that made sense for them, the characters, but that you don’t know what room you entered now, some kind of back room. That was clear from the beginning.”

And, as fantastical as it might sound, she’s clear: it’s all real. “I mean, it’s such a cliché to say that, but everything we see at the end is true at the same time,” she said.

A 1-2 Special release, the film is in limited theaters now, with a wide release to come in February 2027.
